title: Lamb Shank Mafé
localName: Mafé — peanut stew of lamb shanks
author: Pierre Thiam
desc: Six lamb shanks braised in a sauce of tomato paste and a full cup of peanut butter, finished with a spoonful of raw parsley gremolata.
longDesc: Thiam calls lamb shanks slowly simmered in peanut sauce ‘the image of comfort food in Senegal’. The shanks are browned in batches, the onions are taken down with garlic and a diluted tomato paste until the paste is deep dark red, and the peanut butter is whisked into simmering stock a spoonful or two at a time so it dissolves rather than clumps. The shanks go back in under the sauce with a whole Scotch bonnet and fish sauce and cook covered for about an hour and a half, then uncovered until the sauce coats the back of a spoon. A pinch of rof gremolata on each shank at the table cuts the richness.
ingredients: 2 tbsp peanut or vegetable oil, plus more if needed
Salt and freshly ground black pepper for the shanks — quantity not printed in the list
2 tbsp tomato paste, mixed with a few tablespoons of water — amount of water not printed
2 tsp salt and 1 tsp black pepper, for the stock — printed in the method
2 tbsp Vietnamese or Thai fish sauce
Spring vegetable fonio pilaf (SEN058) — quantity not printed
equipment: Large heavy saucepan or Dutch oven
steps: Heat the oil in a large saucepan or Dutch oven over medium-high. Season the shanks with salt and pepper and brown them in batches without crowding the pan, turning to colour all sides — about 8 minutes. Set aside, adding more oil if the pan dries.

In the same pan brown the onions. Lower the heat to low, add the garlic, then the diluted tomato paste. Stir with a wooden spoon for 7 to 10 minutes, until the paste is deep, dark red. Add 1 to 2 tablespoons of water if it starts to scorch.
Pour in the stock, raise the heat to bring it to a boil, then reduce to a simmer. Add the bay leaves, thyme, 2 teaspoons salt and 1 teaspoon pepper.
Add the peanut butter 1 to 2 tablespoons at a time, stirring constantly until each addition is dissolved.

Return the shanks, pressing them down so they are submerged. Add the Scotch bonnet and fish sauce, bring to a boil, reduce to a simmer, cover, and cook about 1 hour 30 minutes, until the shanks are tender.
Uncover and keep cooking until the sauce is thick and coats the back of a spoon. No time is printed for this stage.
Remove the bay leaves, skim the fat, adjust the seasoning.
Serve hot on a platter. Top each shank with a generous pinch of rof gremolata and serve with the fonio pilaf.
chefTips: Add the peanut butter in small spoonfuls and wait for each to dissolve — dumping it in a block gives a grainy, split sauce.
Cook the tomato paste until it is deep dark red before any liquid goes in; it is the colour and the depth of the sauce.

The two printings of this recipe disagree about time: the recipe text says about 1 1/2 hours covered, while the article around it reports the shanks needing about two and a half hours. Judge by the shank — tender, and the meat easy to move on the bone — not by the clock.
The sauce is done when it is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, not before.
Skim the fat at the end; the peanut butter and the lamb both release plenty.
commonMistakes: Adding all the peanut butter at once.
Skipping the browning of the shanks.
Trusting the 90-minute figure on a larger shank without testing for tenderness.
Serving without the gremolata — it is half the point.
storage: 4 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen. The sauce thickens as it cools.
reheating: Low heat, covered, with a splash of water or stock.
healthBenefits: Peanut butter supplies plant protein, monounsaturated fat, and niacin.
Lamb shank is a rich source of iron and zinc.
culturalNote: Mafé is the groundnut stew that most of West Africa claims a version of. In Senegal it is a Sunday and celebration dish, thick enough to need rice or couscous to carry it. Thiam’s version is a restaurant-cook’s mafé, built on a whole shank per guest.
sources: Adapted from ‘Mafé: Savory Peanut Sauce’ (recipe heading ‘Lamb Shank Mafé’), lakeislepress.com. PAGE BYLINE AS PRINTED: ‘Dara O’Brien, Creative Director, Lake Isle Press’ — THE PAGE BYLINE, NOT THE RECIPE’S AUTHOR. CREDITED RECIPE SOURCE: Pierre Thiam with Jennifer Sit, ‘Senegal’ (Lake Isle Press, 2015). DATE: none printed. Yield as printed: ‘Serves 6’. TWO-PASS on every quantity, full agreement.

A second printing, WBUR ‘Here & Now’, 19 October 2015 (also syndicated at NHPR and North Country Public Radio), carries no formal article byline (guest Pierre Thiam, host Jeremy Hobson). Its quantities are SINGLE-PASS because the fetch tool refused quantity transcription on that page; they match the Lake Isle printing on every line.

Doneness cues as printed, in short fragments: tomato paste ‘deep, dark red’; peanut butter ‘until dissolved’; ‘until shanks are tender’; sauce ‘thick and coats the back of a spoon’. No oven or internal temperatures anywhere — heat is given only as medium-high, low and simmer.

UNRECONCILED, WITHIN ONE PAGE: the recipe says ‘about 1 hour 30 minutes’ covered; the blog text around it reports the shanks needing ‘about two and a half hours’. Both are recorded here; neither was picked. Cook time in this entry (165 minutes) is the printed 90 plus the unprinted uncovered reduction, estimated.
